title: Superconducting gap: magnitude, nodes and phase
summary: Read gap measurements with their probe and model. Distinguish an excitation scale from evidence for nodes, relative sign or bulk superconductivity.

review.scope: Edited pinned A5 chapter, selected BCS/Choi and phase-sensitive primary passages, review passages, Hardy/Carbotte abstracts and an independent ideal-DOS state-counting check.
limitations: Selected source checks do not constitute full scientific validation or independent experimental replication.
Hardy is abstract-scoped; tricrystal image fits, uncertainties and all underlying review citations were not independently reproduced.
No sample-specific gap amplitude or transition temperature was re-extracted; calculated gaps are not experimental records.
The DOS check assumes a clean isotropic constant-DOS mean-field model, not a universal tunneling spectrum.
The reporting table still needs row-specific primary-source mapping; selected review passages do not verify all listed controls.

claims.statement: A superconducting gap is an energy scale in a specified excitation spectrum. Its magnitude, momentum dependence and relative phase answer different questions. A suppression of spectral weight is not automatically a superconducting gap, and a fitted gap does not automatically define the temperature of bulk superconductivity. This entry organizes observations and model assumptions rather than ranking materials by a single gap ratio.

claims.statement: The factor above the edge follows from the change of variable $E=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2}$ with the usual Bogoliubov spectral weights. The ideal edge is singular but integrable. A local numerical check integrates it up to a finite energy and recovers the corresponding normal-state $\xi$ interval. The check assumes no lifetime broadening, gap anisotropy or experimental convolution.

claims.statement: In this magnitude-only model, replacing a gap by its negative leaves the excitation energies unchanged. Likewise, independently summing two uncoupled spectral contributions cannot recover their relative sign. This is a limited counterexample to inferring phase from a gap magnitude; it does not say that every interference-sensitive spectrum is phase blind.

claims.statement:
| Probe | Recorded quantity | What must be controlled |
|---|---|---|
| Tunneling or STS | Differential conductance versus bias | Tip and sample spectra, thermal/instrumental broadening, matrix elements and surface variation |
| ARPES | Momentum-resolved photoemission intensity | Occupation, resolution, matrix elements and surface state; a leading edge is not automatically a gap amplitude |
| Optical or THz spectroscopy | Frequency-dependent electrodynamic response | Scattering, multiple bands and the model linking absorption to an excitation threshold |
| Heat capacity | Entropy and bulk excitation contribution | Lattice/magnetic backgrounds and normalization; no direct phase measurement |
| Penetration depth or thermal transport | Low-energy electromagnetic or heat response | Disorder, nonlocality, background and multiple excitation channels |
| Andreev or point-contact spectroscopy | Interface current and conductance | Barrier transparency, heating, contact regime and channel mixing |

claims.statement: A tunnel conductance resembles the sample density of states only with suitable assumptions about the counterelectrode and tunneling matrix element, and after accounting for the thermal convolution. Do not identify every conductance peak with $\Delta$. Photoemission and thermodynamic measurements constrain different aspects of the state; the selected review discusses why magnitude-sensitive probes alone do not measure the relative phase.

claims.statement: Hardy and colleagues report a strong linear term in the penetration-depth change of YBa2Cu3O6.95 single crystals over approximately 3–25 K using a 900 MHz resonator. This is evidence relevant to low-energy excitations under their sample conditions, not a direct measurement of gap phase. The present check covers the publisher abstract.

claims.statement: By contrast, Tsuei and Kirtley use scanning SQUID measurements of NCCO/PCCO tricrystals to test phase-sensitive predictions. Their designed frustrated geometry produces a half-flux signal, while two unfrustrated NCCO geometries serve as controls. The inference depends on junction geometry and the associated model, not merely on observing a spectral dip. Selected author-manuscript passages and the control description were checked; the image fits were not independently reproduced.

claims.statement: Nodes, relative sign and topology are distinct. A low-temperature power law can constrain low-energy excitations without uniquely selecting a pairing representation. A fully open gap on each Fermi-surface sheet can coexist with a relative sign change between sheets. Disorder and sample inhomogeneity must be considered before translating a temperature dependence into a symmetry assignment.

claims.statement: A zero-bias feature alone is not a unique topology test. Identify its field, temperature, position and junction dependence, then compare explicit alternative models. Likewise, a spectroscopic gap-closing temperature must not silently replace a resistive or thermodynamic $T_c$ in a gap ratio. These are inference and reporting limits, not a claim that one alternative explains every observed feature.

claims.statement: Choi and colleagues' MgB2 result is an anisotropic Eliashberg calculation of distinct band-dependent gap scales. Treat those calculated gaps as theory and compare them with separately identified measurements. The pinned chapter's DOI was mismatched; the correct source is nature00898. That correction does not validate a universal multiband gap ratio or independently reproduce the calculation.
